long.hook: Two ways to simulate the same forming test. One is accurate but slow. One is fast but slightly off. And you have one hour of computer time.
long.goal: The goal is a model that predicts the test for any setting, and says how sure it is. Every simulation is one data point.
long.budget: One hour buys about a hundred accurate runs, or about eighteen hundred rough ones. Neither is what you want.
long.three_fine: Spend it all on accurate runs, and you get good points, but too few. Between them, the model guesses, and misses whole features.
long.three_cheap: Spend it all on cheap runs, and the model learns the cheap answer precisely. It becomes confidently wrong.
long.three_mix: Mix them, and the cheap runs draw the shape while a few accurate runs teach the model how far off they are.
long.picking: How were the runs placed? Mostly by a Latin hypercube: spread evenly, decided in advance. We also tried letting the model choose, with integrated variance reduction.
long.results: On a hundred unseen tests, the mix had the lowest error. And when it said ninety-five percent sure, it was right ninety-one percent of the time. Cheap runs alone were right only sixty-eight percent of the time.
long.confirm: Then we wrote the test down in advance and ran twelve fresh trials. The mix won eleven of them, with thirty percent lower error on average.
long.ivr: PLACEHOLDER: filled after the pre-registered IVR run.
long.takeaway: Same hour of compute. About thirty percent less error. And honest about what it doesn't know.

short.s1: Accurate simulations are slow. Cheap ones are fast but slightly off. You have one hour of compute.
short.s2: Accurate only: too few points. Cheap only: confidently wrong. Mixed: cheap runs draw the shape, a few accurate runs fix the offset.
short.s3: Same compute, thirty percent less error, and honest about its uncertainty. Confirmed on twelve pre-registered trials.
